title: If You Stop Attending or Withdraw: What Happens to Your Status
summary: Leaving a school triggers a 14 day notification you owe, and a separate clock on your status. Most advice treats this as unmentionable; the rules are published.
body_html:
Students stop attending for real reasons — money runs out, a family member gets ill, the course turns out to be the wrong one. The usual response to the question is a warning not to let it happen, which is no help once it has.

So here is what the published rules actually say, including the one thing you owe within 14 days whether you intend to stay or not. [source:1]

First: you owe a notification, within 14 days [source:1]

If your institution changes its name or address, ceases to exist, or if you leave it or transfer to another one, you must notify the Commissioner of the Immigration Services Agency within 14 days. [source:1] This applies to mid-to-long-term residents holding Student status, among others. [source:1]

Leaving and transferring are both on that list. [source:1] So the notification is owed whether you quit entirely or move to a different school.

Three things make this easier than it sounds, and all three are on the agency's own page.

You can file it online, through the electronic notification system, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and the system shows your filing history and processing status. [source:1] You can file at a regional immigration office by presenting your residence card. [source:1] Or you can post it, enclosing the notification form and a copy of your residence card. [source:1]

And — this is the part people do not expect — no documents evidencing the notified matter are required. [source:1] You are not assembling a file. You are filing a form.

If you post it, note that the agency does not send any acknowledgement that it was received, and recommends a delivery method you can track. [source:1] Use the online system instead if you can.

Why the notification matters beyond itself

Meeting the notification obligations under the Immigration Act is one of the considerations the agency weighs at renewal, and the affiliated-institution notification is specifically among them. [source:2] The guideline cites Articles 19-7 to 19-13, Article 19-15 and Article 19-16. [source:2]

So the notification is not merely a procedural tidy-up. Filing it is a factor in your favour later; not filing it is a factor against.

This is why the 14 days matter even if your plan is to leave Japan. [source:1] A notification you filed costs you nothing. One you skipped is on the record.

Then: the renewal consideration

Separately from the notification, the agency expects you to have been carrying out the activity your status is for. [source:2]

It names students explicitly. A student who continued residing in Japan after being removed from the register or withdrawing is evaluated as a negative factor, unless there is a legitimate reason for not carrying out the activity. [source:2]

Two words in that sentence do a lot of work.

"Continued residing." The negative factor attaches to staying on after you stopped being a student — not to the act of withdrawing. Someone who withdraws, notifies, and transfers to another school is in a different position from someone who withdraws and stays put.

"Legitimate reason." The exception exists, and the guideline does not define it. We are not going to guess at what qualifies. What we can say is that the exception is written into the rule, so the honest thing to do with a genuine reason is to state it, with evidence, rather than to hope nobody notices.

And: the cancellation clock, which is a different thing

Status cancellation is separate from renewal, and runs on its own grounds under Article 22-4, paragraph 1. [source:3]

Two of them reach a student who has stopped studying.

Ground 5 covers holding a status listed in Appended Table I while not carrying out that status's activity, and residing in Japan carrying out or intending to carry out some other activity instead — absent a legitimate reason. [source:3] Student status is on that table. [source:3]

Ground 6 covers not carrying out the activity of that status for 3 months or more running, absent a legitimate reason. [source:3]

Note the asymmetry between them. Ground 6 is a clock: 3 months. [source:3] Ground 5 has no clock — it turns on whether you are doing something else instead.

Which means the honest answer to "how long can I not attend before there is a problem" is that there are two different answers and only one of them is a number.

What the process looks like if it starts

Before cancellation, an immigration inspector must hear from you, and you may state your case, submit evidence and ask to inspect the materials. [source:3]

For grounds 3 through 10, which includes both of the grounds above, a period of up to 30 days is set for you to leave voluntarily. [source:3] For ground 5 specifically, where there is reasonable cause to suspect you would abscond, deportation proceedings begin immediately instead. [source:3] Not leaving within the period set makes you subject to deportation and to criminal penalty. [source:3]

The difference between a 30 day window and immediate proceedings is conduct during the process. [source:3] That is a reason to answer letters.

What to do, in order

  • Transfer rather than stop, if you can. Transferring is a notified change of institution. [source:1] Stopping and staying is the thing the guideline calls a negative factor. [source:2]
  • File the notification within 14 days regardless. [source:1] Online, no supporting documents, any hour. [source:1] This is the cheapest thing on this page and the one most often skipped.
  • If you have a genuine reason, document it now. Both the renewal consideration and the cancellation grounds carry a legitimate-reason exception. [source:2] [source:3] Medical records and the like are easier to obtain at the time than months later.
  • Talk to the school before you disappear. A school that knows you have a problem can sometimes do something about it. A school recording you as withdrawn cannot.
  • Do not ignore correspondence from immigration. The hearing is your opportunity to submit evidence, and the immediate-deportation route exists for people who appear to be absconding. [source:3]
  • Get advice if it has already gone wrong. A lawyer or an administrative scrivener registered with the immigration bureau, not a forum.

For the full set of renewal considerations, including the tax and insurance items that catch people quietly, see what immigration actually looks at when you renew. If the pressure behind not attending is work hours, what happens if you exceed the work limit covers the same "are you still a student" test from the other side.

This page summarises published rules and guidance; it is not legal advice. The guideline is revised, the exceptions above are decided case by case, and the agency's pages linked below are the authority.

claims_without_sources: 届出を怠った場合の罰則の有無・内容 —— 当該届出ページには罰則の記載がなく、入管法の条文そのものを出典として確認していないため書いていない。更新ガイドラインが「届出義務の履行」を考慮要素に挙げている点のみ出典付きで述べた。
「正当な理由」の具体例 —— 更新ガイドラインも取消しのページも例外を置くが内容を定義していない。推測で書かない。
出席率の数値基準 —— どの出典にも存在しない。巷の「80%」等は書いていない。本文は取消事由の第6号が示す「3か月」という唯一の数値だけを扱った。
退学後に別の学校へ移籍できる条件・時期 —— 学校側の受入れ可否と入管の判断の両方に依存し、公表された基準がない。「移籍は届出対象である」という事実までに留めた。
学費が払えない場合の学校側の対応（分納・猶予の有無）—— 学校ごとに異なり公表もされていない。「学校に相談せよ」とだけ書いた。
